title: The Messianic Banquet
lead: The great feast that God will hold at the end of the age, when the nations eat at his table, death is swallowed up and the righteous eat with the patriarchs and the Messiah (Isaiah 25:6–8; Matthew 8:11; Revelation 19:9).

sections.b:
Covenants and coronations in Israel were sealed with meals. On Sinai the elders "looked upon God, and they ate and drank" (Exodus 24:11), and Israel's kings were crowned with feasts (1 Samuel 11:15; 1 Kings 1:25). Isaiah turns this into a promise for the end: on Mount Zion the LORD of Armies will spread a feast of the richest food and finest wine "for all the peoples," and swallow up death forever (Isaiah 25:6–8; compare Isaiah 55:1–2). Psalm 23:5 pictures God preparing a table for his guest.

Later Jewish writings developed the hope: the righteous eat with the Son of Man (1 Enoch 62:14), Behemoth and Leviathan are kept as food for the last days (2 Baruch 29:4; 4 Ezra 6:49–52), and the Talmud tells of a feast for the righteous made from Leviathan (Bavli Bava Batra 75a). At Qumran the Rule of the Congregation describes a meal at which the Messiah of Israel is present (1QSa II, 11–22). Jesus speaks of many who will come "from the sunrise and the sunset" to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11), tells the parable of the great banquet (Luke 14:15–24), and at the Last Supper looks ahead to drinking the cup new in the kingdom (Matthew 26:29). Revelation calls it "the wedding supper of the Lamb" (Revelation 19:9).
